title: At the feast of Dedication (John 10:22–42)
hook: in winter, at Hanukkah in Solomon's porch, they ask him plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a painting in the catacombs, and the good shepherd who stays when the hireling runs. Your line was I know my own.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." Two little facts, and they set a whole scene. The feast of the dedication is Hanukkah, whose own story is told in First Maccabees, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include. And it's winter, cold enough that Jesus is walking under cover, in the colonnade called Solomon's porch. A crowd gathers close around him there, maybe blocking his way, and asks the question that has followed him for chapters.

First, the feast. Long before Jesus, a Greek king named Antiochus the Fourth set up pagan worship in the temple in Jerusalem and tried to stamp out Jewish practice. A family called the Maccabees led a revolt. When they took back the temple, they cleansed it and dedicated it again, with an eight-day celebration. Hanukkah means dedication. The famous story of a small jar of oil burning for eight days is told later, in the Talmud. Jews keep Hanukkah to this day, lighting lights in winter. So here is Jesus, at the feast that remembers the temple made holy again. The crowd says: "How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." His answer: I've told you, and the works I do tell you. My sheep hear my voice. Then a promise: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Pluck is the King James word; some modern Bibles say snatch, like a wolf grabbing a lamb. And no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand, either. "I and my Father are one." The crowd hears it as blasphemy and picks up stones again. He escapes across the Jordan, to the place where John baptized at the very start, and there, John says, many believed. The story circles back to where it began.
screen: then, large: `I AND MY FATHER ARE ONE.`

segments.voice: If there's a candle or lamp nearby, light it or switch it on; if not, picture one, and watch the light for a moment. Think of someone going through a winter right now, grief, illness, loneliness, fear, and picture them held safe in hands that won't let go, and yourself too, if you're in a winter of your own. If you pray, hold them in the promise that no one can snatch them away; if not, simply keep the light company.
Hanukkah. The Jewish feast of the dedication, remembering the temple cleansed and dedicated again. Jesus walked in the temple at Hanukkah, in winter.
Your line: no one can snatch them. Not from his hand, and not from the Father's. Day six hundred twenty-one, done.

howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights each winter, lighting one more light each night; Christians read this passage as Jesus's plain claim of unity with the Father and a promise that his own are held safe.

chat.says: Wait, Jesus was at Hanukkah? What is that feast actually about?
options: It remembers the temple cleansed and dedicated again after the Maccabees took it back.
It remembers King Solomon building the very first temple, with eight days of lights.
It remembers the escape from Egypt, with a light for each night of the journey.
chat.meaning: Hanukkah means dedication. It remembers the Maccabees cleansing the temple and dedicating it again; John says Jesus walked there at the feast, in winter.

First Maccabees.meaning: a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles telling Hanukkah's story

Solomon's porch.meaning: a covered colonnade at the temple where Jesus walked in winter

Antiochus the Fourth.meaning: the Greek king who set up pagan worship in the temple

Talmud.meaning: a later Jewish work where the oil story is told

blasphemy.meaning: speaking against God; what the crowd heard in his words

notes: 'Only time Hanukkah is mentioned in the Bible's sixty-six books as Protestants count them': First Maccabees (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles) and 2 Maccabees describe its origin. Confirm phrasing.
Rededication date about 164 BC under Judas Maccabeus after Antiochus IV Epiphanes's desecration (167 BC); 'about two centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
Oil miracle first told in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b. Confirm.
Solomon's porch on the temple's east side (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.7). Confirm.
Index carry 'snatch'; KJV 'pluck'. Script explains both.
The Jewish neighbor reference is descriptive, with no comparison. Confirm.
